 Column: Serving as a poll greeter gives new perspective on Election Day 
 Share this:
 Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) 
 Facebook 
 Share on X (Opens in new window) 
 X 
 Poll workers, including from left, RJ Davis, Jeanie Lawson and Kristen Inghram, distribute voter information to those casting their ballots on Election Day, Nov. 4, 2025, at Thalia United Methodist Church in Virginia Beach. (Stephen M. Katz / The Virginian-Pilot) 
 By Clark Murphy | Guest Columnist PUBLISHED: November 18, 2026 at 6:05 PM EST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... “Yes!” “No, thank you. I’m all set!” A silent walk past, occasionally with a disapproving look. Or an emphatic “No chance!”
 These were some of the reactions I received during the recent November elections when I offered voters a Democratic candidate guide outside polling places in Virginia Beach.
 I’ve been a volunteer election poll greeter since 2024, so I’m still learning from longtime volunteers. In only two years, I’ve greeted voters during presidential, congressional, state and local elections, including Virginia Beach School Board and City Council races.
 My job is simple: Greet voters and offer a small guide featuring the names and photos of Democratic-endorsed candidates, along with the specific races they’re running in.
 Sometimes a simple conversation can make a difference. One voter accepted my candidate guide and asked about the three Virginia constitutional amendments on the ballot. She hadn’t had time to read much about them, so I spent a couple of minutes explaining each amendment and why I supported voting “Yes.” She thanked me and went inside to vote. A little later, as she was leaving, she passed me again, smiled and said, “Thank you!”
 Not every experience has been pleasant. One voter walked by as I offered him a candidate guide. He responded, “Why would I be interested in what you have to say?” He seemed angry that I was even there. I didn’t respond. But after voting, he came back and again seemed bothered by my presence. I simply wished him a nice day, and he left.
 You never quite know what reaction you’ll get. I’ve learned not to take an unfriendly response personally. People have different political views, and that’s fine. Whether they agree with me or not, I appreciate everyone who takes the time to vote.
 I’ve also really enjoyed getting to know my fellow Democratic poll greeters. The longtime volunteers have been welcoming, helpful and encouraging to newcomers such as me. When one two-hour shift ends, those leaving share stories and observations with the volunteers arriving for the next shift. We exchange advice, talk about how things have gone and encourage one another. It’s a little community of its own.
 The dedication of candidates has also impressed me. They stand outside polling places for hours, introducing themselves and talking with voters. And that’s in addition to all the hours spent knocking on doors, attending community meetings, speaking at neighborhood gatherings, writing postcards and reaching out to residents.
 Regardless of political affiliation, I admire their willingness to put themselves forward and serve their communities. I’ve come to appreciate just how much these candidates give of themselves, whether they win or lose.
 I’ve also seen some encouraging examples of people treating one another with respect. Sometimes candidates approach poll greeters supporting their opponents, introduce themselves, shake hands and exchange a few friendly words.
 In a recent Substack essay “When did respect become partisan?” newly elected Virginia Beach School Board member Antoinette Kahan reflected on her experiences campaigning and the importance of treating people with respect, even when we disagree. She wrote, “But we can decide that disagreement need not become disrespect.”
 I couldn’t agree more.
 If you’ve ever thought about volunteering during an election, I’d encourage you to give poll greeting a try. It’s a great way to support candidates you believe in, and even a weekly two-hour shift can be rewarding. You’ll meet interesting people, share a few laughs and maybe even come away with a story or two of your own.
 I’ve come to appreciate not only the people who vote, but also the candidates and volunteers who make our elections possible. Whether you greet me with a smile, a polite refusal, a frown or an emphatic “No chance,” I’m glad you came to vote.
 And I’ll look forward to seeing you at the next election.
 Clark Murphy lives and votes in Virginia Beach, where he also teaches English as a Second Language to college students.
